Virgin Island French grunts

Teague Bay, St. Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands
migratory tradition
MigrationForaging

Fish “exhibit social traditions of daytime schooling sites and twilight migration routes.” Social groups prefer to rest at given coral heads and routes to seagrass beds to forage at dusk (Helfman & Schultz 1984)

Vertical: Inferred yesHorizontal: Inferred yesOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Fish “exhibit social traditions of daytime schooling sites and twilight migration routes.” Social groups prefer to rest at given coral heads and routes to seagrass beds to forage at dusk (Helfman & Schultz 1984)

Vertical: "Large juveniles (40-120 mm total length, 80-700 days old) form coral-head-specific daytime resting schools that persist for as long as 3 years, although members of these schools do not exceed 2 years in age (Brothers & McFarland 1981; Helfman et al. 1982)." (Helfman & Schultz 1984); "Many fish, for example, have traditional breeding, feeding and resting grounds, and the migration routes taken between these locations are often highly conserved over multiple generations" (Brown & Webster 2025)

Horizontal: Transplantation experiment showed that transplanted fish adopted local foraging routes when mixed with original resident fish, while those without the opportunity to interact with residents maintained similar routes to their original location (Helfman & Schultz 1984)

Domains: migration, foraging

Sources: [1] [2]
